top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B011) rests on one two-author 1997 mechanism: credit limits tied to collateral values, and collateral values that depend on credit, turn small temporary shocks into large and persistent cycles. The idea is general, has been reused for nearly three decades, and needs no arbitrary boundary drawn through a diffuse literature. The 2022 overlap with the banks-and-crises prize is mainly a citation-wording question, because the collateral-price feedback is distinct from bank runs and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator. The main weakness is indirect identification: the channel is established as a mechanism, not as a measured magnitude. The citation should therefore credit the mechanism and make no claim about effect size. P002 (Helpman and Melitz, B005) is a close second. Its selection and reallocation margins are tested more directly on firm-level data, but attribution is harder because of the uncredited Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, Krugman's 2008 prize, and the need to separate Helpman's marginal credit from his other work. I would support P002 if the committee judges the 2022 overlap decisive against P001. P003 (B014) is well replicated but may combine two achievements, leaves out Dorn and Acemoglu-Restrepo, and has contested China-shock magnitudes. A sound award of any of the three is preferable to no award, so P000 is last. This assessment relies on the supplied committee text and general knowledge, and I have not independently verified any source.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile: it lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Hanson or Katz. My work with Lindvall and Cermeño on state capacity and railroads is field-adjacent to B012, which is not on the final slate.
